title: Guru Angad's gurpurab
hookLine: his birth is remembered with Gurmukhi and the langar of Mata Khivi

lines: A HOT PLATE ON THE FLOOR.
cards: Two things in Sikh life touch almost everyone, every day, and you barely notice them. One is the shape of the letters: every gutka, the street signs of Indian Punjab, every line of scripture on your phone in Gurmukhi.

The other is the free kitchen: a hot plate of dal and roti, served to anyone who sits down on the floor. A script and a kitchen. Sikh memory ties both, in a special way, to one couple in a village called Khadur.

teach.b: Guru Angad was born in 1504 and named Lehna. He was a devotee of the goddess Durga, tradition says, until he heard a Sikh reciting Guru Nanak's hymns, and went to find the Guru at Kartarpur.
He served him so completely that Guru Nanak named him his successor and gave him a new name: Angad, from ang, a limb, part of the Guru's own body.
You heard it from Satta and Balvand a couple of weeks ago: same light, new body. As Guru, he settled at Khadur, and two things grew there.
The first is Gurmukhi. Tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping and spreading the script the Guru's words are written in, so that ordinary people, not only scholars, could read them.
Historians discuss how much of the script existed before him, but Sikhs remember him as the one who put it in children's hands.
The second is the langar, and here the credit goes to his wife, Mata Khivi.
She ran the kitchen at Khadur, feeding everyone who came. Satta and Balvand praise her in their var, on Ang nine sixty-seven.
In paraphrase: Khivi, a good woman, gives shade like a leafy tree; she serves rice pudding rich with ghee. Sikhs remember her as the mother of the langar. His gurpurab falls in spring.
Many gurdwaras mark it with kirtan, some with Gurmukhi classes for children, and of course the kitchen is open.

how: On Guru Angad's gurpurab in spring, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and some hold Gurmukhi classes, remembering the script he spread and Mata Khivi's kitchen at Khadur.

games.q: you're the second Guru at Khadur, and the Guru's hymns are spreading. how do you help ordinary people read them?
o: shape and spread a simple script, and teach it to children.
have them memorized only, never written.
games.why: tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping and spreading Gurmukhi, so anyone, not only scholars, could read the Guru's words.

practice: With a pen, or a finger on the table, draw oorhaa, the first letter of the Gurmukhi alphabet, slowly, once and then again; if you can't see it on a screen, draw the first letter of your own name with the same care.
Wobbly is fine, since every child's first one is, so think of everyone who learned to read the Guru's words from that letter. If you pray, you can say Waheguru when you finish.
